title: What Happens in the 2 Seconds After You Tap Your Card
description:
You tap your card, it beeps, and two seconds later your coffee is approved. But in those two seconds, a tiny message travels from the chip in your card to a payment processor, across a card network, to your bank and back. This video follows that trip, explains why "approved" is not the same as "paid," and slices a $5 coffee to show who takes a cut: U.S. merchants paid $198.25 billion in card processing fees in 2025, about 1.59% of every purchase on average.

In this video:
- Hook: a $5 coffee and a two-second beep
- Time freezes: following the glowing message
- Stop 1: inside the chip (how a card with no plug wakes up and makes a one-time code)
- Stop 2: the payment processor and the acquiring bank
- Stop 3: the card network highway (and the fee called interchange)
- Stop 4: the issuing bank's three questions and the hold
- Back at the counter: approved, but not paid yet
- That night: batching and settlement (1 to 3 business days)
- Slicing the $5 coffee: about 8 cents in fees, and who gets each slice
- Who really pays: one price tag for everyone
- The cash customer: cash fell from 33% to 14% of payments (2015 to 2025)
- What this means for you: three ideas worth keeping
- Wrap-up

Our own calculations:
[D1] $5.00 x 1.59% = 7.95 cents, about 8 cents. This is a national average across all cards and sales; fees on a single small purchase can be higher because many pricing plans add a fixed per-transaction charge.
[D2] Network fees of 0.1% to 0.2% on $5 = 0.5 to 1 cent, so "a penny or less."
Real fees vary by card, merchant, and sale size. The Boston Fed figure ($149 per cash-using household per year) is from an older 2010 study.
